lead: A sensor turns a physical quantity — light, distance, temperature — into a voltage or digital pulse. A board reads it on a pin, compares it with a rule and switches an actuator: LED, buzzer, relay or motor. This chapter covers common IoT interface circuits — LED resistor, push button, voltage divider, ultrasonic ranger, temperature sensor — and drivers for 12 V lamps or motors. The pattern runs door alarms, water-level cutoffs, smart parking and cold-chain monitors.
prereq: You need pinMode, digitalWrite and digitalRead from Chapter 4.2, Raspberry Pi GPIO from Chapter 4.3, and the voltage divider idea.

sections.h3: Digital pins: LEDs and push buttons

blocks.text: Every board exposes digital pins. As output, a pin is 0 V (LOW) or logic voltage (HIGH): 5 V on most Arduinos, 3.3 V on a Raspberry Pi. As input, it reports whether voltage is above or below about half logic voltage. One bit drives an LED or reads a button.

An LED needs a series resistor: R = (Vsupply − Vf) ÷ I, where Vf is forward voltage (about 2 V red, 3.2 V blue), I is current in amperes. For 5 V, red LED and 10 mA: R=(5−2)÷0.01=300 Ω; use 330 Ω. Keep an Arduino pin at or below 20 mA; more needs a transistor.

A bare push button leaves the pin floating when open. Connect one side to the pin and the other to GND, then pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP). The pin reads HIGH when open and LOW when pressed; forgetting inversion is a common bug. Contacts bounce for milliseconds, so ignore repeats for about 20 ms.

An analog sensor returns a varying voltage; the ADC converts it to a number. Arduino Uno ADC is 10-bit against 5 V. There are 1024 steps (2¹⁰) across the reference, so one step is Vref ÷ 1024 ≈ 4.9 mV. The code formula V = reading × Vref ÷ 1023 maps largest reading 1023 to full scale; both appear because step count is 1024 but codes run 0–1023. reading is analogRead(), 0 to 1023. Raspberry Pi has no ADC, so it uses an external chip such as MCP3008 (see Chapter 4.4).

blocks.where: Vout is the midpoint voltage sent to the ADC pin; Vcc is the supply, 5 V; R_LDR is the LDR resistance in ohms; R is the fixed resistor in ohms.

blocks.text: An LDR (light-dependent resistor) drops resistance as light rises — roughly 1 MΩ dark and 1 kΩ bright. A pin reads voltage, not resistance, so use a divider: LDR from 5 V to midpoint, fixed R from midpoint to GND. With R = 10 kΩ, dark gives 5×10÷1010≈0.05 V; bright gives 5×10÷11≈4.55 V. Light level rises with voltage.
LM35 outputs 10 mV per °C and 0 V at 0 °C. T = Vout ÷ 0.01 V/°C; 0.303 V means 30.3 °C. At 4.9 mV per ADC step, one count is about 0.49 °C, so good to about half a degree.

DHT11 and DHT22 are digital: one wire carries a 40-bit burst of humidity and temperature, decoded by a library. DHT11: 0–50 °C to ±2 °C and 20–90 % RH to ±5 %. DHT22: −40 to 80 °C to ±0.5 °C and 0–100 % RH to ±2 %. Read DHT11 at most once a second and DHT22 once every two seconds, or they return errors.
A pin supplies only a few milliamperes; lamps, pumps and motors need more. An actuator sits behind a driver, and the pin drives the driver.

items: Buzzer: an active buzzer has its own oscillator, so digitalWrite(pin, HIGH) starts a fixed tone; a passive buzzer needs tone(pin, 2000) for 2 kHz. Small buzzers that draw under about 20 mA can be driven from a pin directly; anything that draws more (many buzzers draw 25–40 mA, and the Arduino per-pin recommended limit is 20 mA) needs a transistor driver, the same as a loud buzzer.

Relay: a 5 V coil closes contacts in a separate circuit — a 230 V lamp or a pump. A ready-made module contains the driver transistor and a flyback diode that absorbs the coil's inductive kick at switch-off. Contacts carry a rating such as 10 A at 250 V AC. Mains wiring is dangerous: keep it enclosed and switch off before touching.

DC motor: an H-bridge driver (L293D, L298N, TB6612) sits between the pin and the motor, with its own supply and a shared ground. Two pins set direction, and analogWrite() with PWM from 0 to 255 sets speed.

blocks.text: The control pattern is read, compare, act. One threshold makes a relay chatter near the boundary, so use two: on below 19 cm, off above 21 cm. The gap is hysteresis; it protects relay and load.

Boards do not share logic voltage. Arduino Uno pins are 5 V. Raspberry Pi GPIO is 3.3 V and not 5 V tolerant: a 5 V signal can destroy it; a 3.3 V output may be too low for some 5 V modules to read HIGH.

blocks.where: Vin is the incoming signal voltage; R1 is the resistor from Vin to the midpoint; R2 is the resistor from midpoint to GND; Vout is the reduced voltage reaching the pin.

blocks.text: Three fixes: choose a 3.3 V sensor; use a resistive divider for one-way high-to-low; or use a bidirectional MOSFET level-shifter for two-way lines such as I²C. For 5 V with R1=1 kΩ and R2=2 kΩ, Vout=5×2÷3=3.33 V, safe for Pi. Power is a second gap: Pi 3.3 V pins give little current, so motors and relays take own supply with common ground.

spec.aria: An ultrasonic sensor sends a pulse to an object at 9.95 centimetres and it returns, on a distance scale to 25 centimetres with a dashed alarm line at 20; below, the echo pulse 580 microseconds wide and the distance working.

examples.question: An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor is connected to an Arduino. The sketch sends a 10 µs trigger pulse and the echo pin stays HIGH for 580 µs. Take the speed of sound as 343 m/s. (a) Find the distance to the object in metres and in centimetres. (b) The sketch sounds a buzzer when the distance is below 20 cm. Does the buzzer sound?
steps: Convert echo time: t = 580 µs = 580 × 10⁻⁶ s = 5.80 × 10⁻⁴ s.
The pulse travels to the object and back, so path = v × t = 343 × 5.80 × 10⁻⁴ m.
9.947 cm < 20 cm, so the buzzer sounds.
examples.answer: The object is 0.09947 m (9.947 cm, about 9.95 cm) away; this is below 20 cm, so the buzzer sounds.
examples.check:
v = 343.0
t_us = 580.0
t = t_us * 1e-6
d = v * t / 2
print(round(d, 5))
print(round(d * 100, 3))

traps: Using the whole echo time as a one-way distance doubles the answer. Always divide by 2 after multiplying speed by time.
Mixing microseconds and seconds: 580 µs is 580 × 10⁻⁶ s, not 580 s; convert before multiplying by 343 m/s.
Forgetting the LED series resistor, or sizing it from the supply alone. Use R = (Vsupply − Vf) ÷ I, not Vsupply ÷ I.
Assuming INPUT_PULLUP gives HIGH when pressed. It gives LOW when pressed, because the button shorts the pin to ground.
Feeding a 5 V sensor output straight into Raspberry Pi GPIO. The Pi is 3.3 V only; reduce the level with a divider or a level shifter first.

quiz.q: State the voltage resolution of a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference.
quiz.a: There are 1024 steps (2¹⁰) across 5 V, so one step is 5 V ÷ 1024 ≈ 4.9 mV. The code formula V = reading × 5 ÷ 1023 maps reading 1023 to full scale.

quiz.q: Why does an LED need a series resistor when driven from a GPIO pin?
quiz.a: An LED has a nearly fixed forward drop and very little internal resistance, so current would rise until the pin or LED is damaged. The resistor drops the remaining voltage and sets I = (Vsupply − Vf) ÷ R.

quiz.q: An LM35 (10 mV/°C) is read by a 10-bit, 5 V Arduino ADC and analogRead() returns 62. Find the temperature.
An HC-SR04 echo stays HIGH for 1160 µs. Take v = 343 m/s and the buzzer threshold as 20 cm. Find the distance and state whether the buzzer sounds.
quiz.a: t = 1160 × 10⁻⁶ s; v × t = 343 × 0.00116 = 0.39788 m; d = 0.39788 ÷ 2 = 0.19894 m = 19.9 cm. Since 19.9 cm < 20 cm, the buzzer sounds, but only just.

quiz.q: A 5 V ultrasonic module's echo pin is wired directly to a Raspberry Pi GPIO. Explain the risk and give a divider that fixes it.
quiz.a: The Pi GPIO is 3.3 V logic and not 5 V tolerant, so 5 V can destroy the input stage. Use R1 = 1 kΩ from echo to the GPIO node and R2 = 2 kΩ from that node to GND: Vout = 5 × 2 ÷ (1 + 2) = 3.33 V, which is safe.

quiz.q: Why does a relay module include a flyback diode across the coil?
quiz.a: The coil is an inductor. When the driver switches off, the collapsing field produces a large reverse voltage spike that can destroy the transistor. The diode gives that current a safe path.

quiz.q: A fan switches on at 30 °C and off at 29.9 °C, and the relay clicks rapidly. Explain the cause and the fix.
quiz.a: The two thresholds are so close that sensor noise crosses them repeatedly. Widen the band, for example on at 31 °C and off at 29 °C, so the relay changes state only on a real change; this hysteresis also protects the contacts.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry these circuits grow into sensor nodes with isolated inputs, opto-couplers and industrial 4–20 mA loops, because long wires pick up noise that a breadboard never shows. Hobby boards are replaced by boards with protected I/O and watchdog timers. Search for 'opto-isolated relay module', '4–20 mA current loop sensor' and 'level shifter BSS138' to see the next step, and read datasheet absolute maximum ratings before connecting anything expensive.
